issue.title: etcd: extend rate limiting to consider the number of inflight requests

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: There is a performance impact of this.

labels.name: release-note/minor
labels.description: This PR changes functionality that users may find relevant to operating Cilium.

labels.name: ready-to-merge
labels.description: This PR has passed all tests and received consensus from code owners to merge.

issue.body:
Reporting the description of the last commit for convenience:

```
Currently, the etcd rate limiter operates based on a token bucket of a
fixed size. Yet, this is problematic when etcd is overloaded, since we
may continue to issue new requests even if it cannot keep up. Hence,
let's start using the custom APILimiter, which also takes into account
the number of currently inflight requests. The maximum amount of
inflight requests can configured through the etcd.maxInflight parameter,
and defaults to the same value as etcd.qps if unset.
```

<!-- Description of change -->

```release-note
etcd: extend rate limiting to consider the number of inflight requests
```

issue.title: Clustermesh-apiserver: CiliumEndpoint out of order deletions leads to dropping packets for valid network policies

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: This is a bug in the Cilium logic.

labels.name: kind/community-report
labels.description: This was reported by a user in the Cilium community, eg via Slack.

labels.name: area/clustermesh
labels.description: Relates to multi-cluster routing functionality in Cilium.

labels.name: stale

issue.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### What happened?

After cycling several thousand pods at once we observed cilium reporting dropped packets with the reason `Policy Denied` to pods running in other clusters joined together with clustermesh that should have been allowed.

We traced this down to the clustermesh-apiservers in the cluster where the destination pods were hosted. The destination pod IPs were correct, the ciliumendpoint CRs existed, however some IPs were missing from clustermesh-apiserver kvstore (etcd sidecar container). This was observed well after clustermesh-apiserver finished processing its queue of events.

We have concluded this happens due to a combination of ip reuse and deletion events being processed out of order by clustermesh-apiserver.

Under heavy load (many ciliumendpoint create/update/delete events)  the clustermesh-apiserver is unable to keep up with the queue which leads to backpressure on the watch connection. Eventually the watcher fails which leads to a re-list where create events get re-queued and processed before delete events.

When an IP is reused and the creation of the new ciliumendpoints is processed before the deletion of the old ciliumendpoints the clustermesh-apiserver blindly deletes the ip from the kvstore since the keys are identical (e.g. `cilium/state/ip/v1/default/100.10.10.10`). The only way to recover from this state was to restart the clustermesh-apiservers to resync the ciliumendpoints or restart the impacted pods to create new ciliumendpoints.

#### What I expect to happen

I would expect cilium to handle out of order deletions properly. This could be accomplished by doing a comparison of the `namespace/pod` stored in the value against that in the ciliumendpoint before doing the delete. And only deleting when the `namespace/pod` are the same.

I also noticed the clustermesh-apiserver is using an informer directly to process events while doing blocking operations which is a big contributor to the backpressure/failure we are observing. Using a [workqueue](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue) or [controller](https://pkg.go.dev/sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime@v0.14.6/pkg/controller#Controller) would help process these events without blocking to help mitigate the issue and improve performance.

1. Initially observed on EKS and reproduced using KIND
2. Clustermesh-apiserver enabled using CRDs to propigate endpoints
3. I've included a bash script I used to reproduce the issue in a local kind cluster. It performs the following:

#### Steps to reproduce
1. Create a ciliumendpoint `endpoint1` with the ip 100.10.10.10.
2. Generate load by creating and deleting 5000 ciliumendpoints
3. Delete `endpoint1`
4. Generate load by creating and deleting 5000 ciliumendpoints
5. Create a ciliumendpoint `endpoint2` with the ip 100.10.10.10 (same ip).
6. Observe the output of watching the key
```bash
etcdctl --cert etcd.crt --cacert etcd-ca.crt --key etcd.key watch cilium/state/ip/v1/default/100.10.10.10
PUT
cilium/state/ip/v1/default/100.10.10.10
{"IP":"100.10.10.10","Mask":null,"HostIP":"","ID":0,"Key":0,"Metadata":"","K8sNamespace":"default","K8sPodName":"endpoint2"}
DELETE
```
<details>
<summary>Bash script to reproduce race condition</summary>

```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -e

total_ciliumendpoints=5000
batch_size=100

# Extract etcd client credentials
kubectl -n kube-system get secret clustermesh-apiserver-remote-cert -o json | jq -r '.data["tls.crt"]' | base64 -d > etcd.crt
kubectl -n kube-system get secret clustermesh-apiserver-remote-cert -o json | jq -r '.data["tls.key"]' | base64 -d > etcd.key
kubectl -n kube-system get secret clustermesh-apiserver-remote-cert -o json | jq -r '.data["ca.crt"]' | base64 -d > etcd-ca.crt

# Start the kubectl port-forward in the background
kubectl -n kube-system port-forward svc/clustermesh-apiserver 2379:2379 > /dev/null &

# Store the process ID of the background process
port_forward_pid=$!

# Function to clean up the background process when the script finishes
cleanup() {
  kill $port_forward_pid
}

check_etcd() {
    echo
    echo "Checking etcd:"
    sleep 1
    etcdctl --cert etcd.crt --cacert etcd-ca.crt --key etcd.key get cilium/state/ip/v1/default/100.10.10.10
    echo
}

# Register the cleanup function to be called on script exit
trap cleanup EXIT

ENDPOINT_YAML=""

generate_ciliumendpoint_yaml() {
  local index=$1
  cat <<EOF
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEndpoint
metadata:
  name: endpoint-$index
status:
  networking:
    addressing:
    - ipv4: 10.10.10.$index
EOF
}

apply_ciliumendpoints_batch() {
  local start=$1
  local end=$2
  local batch_yaml=""
  for ((i = start; i < end; i++)); do
    yaml=$(generate_ciliumendpoint_yaml $i)
    batch_yaml+="$yaml"$'\n---'$'\n'  # Separate YAMLs with '---' and add newline
  done
  echo "$batch_yaml" | kubectl apply -f -
}

delete_ciliumendpoints_batch() {
  local start=$1
  local end=$2
  local batch_yaml=""
  for ((i = start; i < end; i++)); do
    yaml=$(generate_ciliumendpoint_yaml $i)
    batch_yaml+="$yaml"$'\n---'$'\n'  # Separate YAMLs with '---' and add newline
  done
  echo "$batch_yaml" | kubectl delete --wait=false -f -
}

generate_load() {
    for ((start = 0; start < total_ciliumendpoints; start += batch_size)); do
    end=$((start + batch_size))
    if ((end > total_ciliumendpoints)); then
        end=$total_ciliumendpoints
    fi

    echo "Applying CiliumEndpoints batch: $start - $((end - 1))"
    apply_ciliumendpoints_batch $start $end
    done

    for ((start = 0; start < total_ciliumendpoints; start += batch_size)); do
    end=$((start + batch_size))
    if ((end > total_ciliumendpoints)); then
        end=$total_ciliumendpoints
    fi

    echo "Applying CiliumEndpoints batch: $start - $((end - 1))"
    delete_ciliumendpoints_batch $start $end
    done
}

create_endpoint1(){
endpoint1='
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEndpoint
metadata:
  name: endpoint1
status:
  networking:
    addressing:
    - ipv4: 100.10.10.10
'
echo "$endpoint1" | kubectl apply -f -
}

create_endpoint1
check_etcd
generate_load
kubectl delete ciliumendpoint/endpoint1
check_etcd
sleep 5
generate_load

# Create second endpoint with the same IP.
endpoint2='
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEndpoint
metadata:
  name: endpoint2
status:
  networking:
    addressing:
    - ipv4: 100.10.10.10
'
echo "$endpoint2" | kubectl apply -f -

etcdctl --cert etcd.crt --cacert etcd-ca.crt --key etcd.key watch cilium/state/ip/v1/default/100.10.10.10

# Clean up endpoint2 before running again.
# kubectl delete ciliumendpoint/endpoint2
```

</details>

### Cilium Version

1.12.3

### Kernel Version

5.4.228-132.418.amzn2.x86_64

### Kubernetes Version

Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23+", GitVersion:"v1.23.16-eks-48e63af", GitCommit:"e6332a8a3feb9e0fe3db851878f88cb73d49dd7a", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2023-01-24T19:18:15Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

We frequently see logs from the `DeltaFIFO Pop Process` saying `slow event handlers blocking the queue`.

body: I just realized that this performance issue was actually a reason why we have seen such a huge improvement in Kubernetes when we started limiting max number of events attached to a single lease (10x CPU reduction of Etcd): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/98257#issuecomment-772478066

Thanks for the detailed report and repro @marseel :)

I've been quickly running this through a profiler with the following result:

![image](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/assets/85170409/e6d22f7c-f664-4c1f-9f56-182c884d927f)

That should be relatively simple to optimize, it's mostly on the creating a slice from a map which is then checked individually per key. 

https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/004195bb6eac3ddf2646ff0ac2c56654bb3ceda5/server/etcdserver/apply/apply_auth.go#L125-L136


This TODO also looks like a nice candidate to optimize: 

https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/004195bb6eac3ddf2646ff0ac2c56654bb3ceda5/server/auth/store.go#L847-L850

Thanks for looking into this.

I think it explains why I've seen different results in this repro and our production cluster.
If I understand correctly, my repro doesn't use auth, but the production setup does - that's why I have seen such a big difference in QPS between production and repro.
For our use case, it would make sense to have a "short" path that checks if a user is a root only once instead of for all keys - https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/fbed8cb645918b3c1955fb446ac3d31940b3c9f3/server/auth/store.go#L873

So maybe something like, `isAuthDisabledOrRootUser` before this loop: https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/41ff2370e98740e3ef0f788b3fea5379258c7090/server/etcdserver/apply/apply_auth.go#L128

I spoke a little too soon about the simplicity of the fix, this is actually a much bigger story for the following reasons.

1. Keys() as a string slices

As you can see most of the time we're spending on converting between string and byte slices here. Map keys can't be `[]byte`, so I assume this is why a `string` key has been chosen instead. The map and its amortized O(1) access also makes sense, especially in the attach/detach scenarios. 

Because etcd is only `[]byte` everywhere, there's a significant toll on converting it back and forth here and in many other places around the `Lease`. What do you folks think about using a different `map` implementation?

Obviously, the `IsPutPermitted` would also require a batched version where we pass multiple keys. 

2. runtime enable/disable of auth

It's a cool feature, but it seems we have to continuously check for auth. Otherwise we could just switch out the `authBackend` entirely and skip all the overhead it comes with.

---

I wrote a little mitigation that would (at least) fix it for the cases where auth is not enabled:
https://github.com/tjungblu/etcd/commit/dff670b423e5688d0a6de37f0a4d008347211536

which I assume would be most relevant for k8s anyway. Let me know if this is too pragmatic :safety_pin:

> If I understand correctly, my repro doesn't use auth, but the production setup does - that's why I have seen such a big difference in QPS between production and repro.

ah gotcha, how are you configuring etcd in that case?

Similar, but with auth enabled and only the root user is writing keys. As we can see here: https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/fbed8cb645918b3c1955fb446ac3d31940b3c9f3/server/auth/store.go#L873
permission checks for root user and does not depend on key value so we could have short path for it too.

luckily there's a check for that already:

https://github.com/tjungblu/etcd/commit/014b17d3d0f2e87ca40a338a1b8e16e1f26730cc#diff-85ead21002d52058142cc354a8367cfe808d7a5d7cdc65ff315aa84edb947c48R128-R132

but yeah, let's hear the thoughts of the others. I think this would be a much bigger refactoring otherwise.
lgtm from my point of view. Thanks!

issue.title: kvstore: limit keys attached to single lease, and react to expiration

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: There is a performance impact of this.

labels.name: ready-to-merge
labels.description: This PR has passed all tests and received consensus from code owners to merge.

labels.name: area/clustermesh
labels.description: Relates to multi-cluster routing functionality in Cilium.

labels.name: release-note/misc
labels.description: This PR makes changes that have no direct user impact.

issue.body:
Reporting the description of the first commit for convenience:

***
Currently, each etcd client is associated with a single session, and the
corresponding lease is attached to all upserted keys (if the lease
parameter is set). This approach, though, suffers from performance
issues, because put requests in etcd take linear apply time depending
on the number of keys already attached to the lease (https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15993).
This performance penalty is planned to be fixed in etcd (at least for the
common case in which the user which performs the request has root role).

In the meanwhile, let's make sure that we attach a limited number of
keys to a single lease. In particular, this commit introduces the etcd
lease manager, which is responsible for managing the lease acquisitions,
tracking the keys that are attached to each of them. Once the number of
keys per lease exceeds the configured threshold, a new lease gets
automatically acquired. The lease usage counter is decremented when a
given key gets deleted. Finally, in case one of the leases fails to be
renewed, the manager allows to emit a notification event for all the keys
that were attached to it.
***

Additionally, the sync store implementation is modified to register for the lease expiration events, appropriately triggering the re-creation of the given keys. This allows to mitigate the possibility that keys get deleted because the associated lease failed to be renewed.
